newsitem.title: USA: Poll cripples San Antonio Spurs's new stadium plan.
newsitem.headline: Poll cripples San Antonio Spurs's new stadium plan.

text.p: The San Antonio Spurs' hopes of winning a new basketball arena have been crippled by a new opinion poll showing that voters would not approve spending tax dollars on the proposed stadium.

Commissioned by the Spurs franchise, the poll of 773 registered voters in Bexar County showed that 61 percent rejected the idea of putting up any public money for the stadium, which would cost about $120 million.
It was the third such poll commissioned by the team in as many years. All showed similar results.
"We have a disconnect, and frankly, I don't know what to do about it," Spurs Chairman of the Board Peter M. Holt said in a statement late on Tuesday.

The franchise had been encouraged by a new state law which allows public funding for sports facilities so long as they are approved by voters. The law provides numerous financing options including a hike in the sales tax or using revenues from car rental and hotel-motel taxes.
But 68 percent of those questioned in the poll released late Tuesday opposed increasing the sales tax by half a cent for three to five years.
And 64 percent opposed a so-called tourist tax which would raise rental car tax from 10 percent to 15 percent and the hotel occupancy tax from 15 percent to 17 percent.
Holt said 75 percent of those polled said the Spurs are an asset to the community and 70 percent think it is important to keep the team in the city.
"But no matter what the scenario, 61 percent have hardened attitudes against a new coliseum," he said.

"I'm through having this issue of coliseums, locations and elections dominate all our attention," Holt added. "We, and I mean all of us in this community, are back to square one with a problem that still needs to be resolved."

The Spurs currently play in the city-owned Alamodome under a 10-year lease, which can be terminated under notice. The Alamodome, built at a cost of $150 million, is five years old and city officials would like the Spurs to stay there.
But Spurs officials say the dome is more suited for football and other major sports rather than basketball. They said the dome arrangement will not be able to meet the future costs of the franchise.
Ronaldo Bono, San Antonio's assistant city manager, said the city is willing to sit down with the Spurs to discuss refurbishing the dome to meet the team's needs.
"We certainly are interested in working with them (the Spurs) to ensure their viability," Bono told Reuters on Wednesday.
But Patti Larsen, a spokeswoman for the Spurs, said such discussions in the past have not been productive.
"It is now up to the community and the leadership to come up with a plan that the Spurs can be a part of. We cannot originate any plans to make the franchise viable," she said.

Larsen said the team's owners are committed to keeping the Spurs in the city but the future cannot be predicted. "They (the owners) cannot change laws of economics in the future that will keep the Spurs viable," she said.
